Auth.Simple.name: Auth.Simple
Auth.Simple.comment:
Exploring the structure of the package...

# Tables

## Base tables

These tables are the tables that are necessary to be created
and exist with a specific schema (minimal schema) for the auth
to work at all.

- `users` - user data, can be augmented after this with more data
- `sessions` - login session; method-agnostic
- `auth_events` - event log for auditing; can be disabled?

## Unknown... TBD

I'm not sure if these tables are method-specific or just part of
the base tables? I could create them and they could just be empty?

- `user_usernames`
- `user_emails`

## Password-specific method

These are only needed if the password auth method is added to the
database.

- `passwords`
- `password_reset_tokens`

Auth.Simple.AuthEvent.name: Auth.Simple.AuthEvent

unions.name: AuthEventType
unions.comment:
The closed set of authentication events this package records.

This is package-owned, not consumer-extensible: an auth event is always one of
these known kinds. Each maps to a stable snake_case string stored in the
`event_type` column (see [`eventTypeToString`](#eventTypeToString)).

aliases.name: AuthEvent
aliases.comment: A row from the `auth_events` table. `userId` and `metadata` are nullable.
aliases.type: { id : String.String, userId : Maybe.Maybe String.String, eventType : Auth.Simple.AuthEvent.AuthEventType, occurredAt : Basics.Int, metadata : Maybe.Maybe String.String }

values.name: create
values.comment:
Record a new auth event and save it to the database.

Generates a fresh `id` and an `occurred_at` timestamp of now, inserts the row, and
returns the created [`AuthEvent`](#AuthEvent). To insert inside an existing
transaction with a caller-supplied `id` and timestamp, use [`insert`](#insert)
directly.
values.type: { userId : Maybe.Maybe String.String, eventType : Auth.Simple.AuthEvent.AuthEventType, metadata : Maybe.Maybe String.String } -> Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error Auth.Simple.AuthEvent.AuthEvent

values.name: delete
values.comment:
Delete an auth event by `id`.

Provided for completeness; removing an audit record is atypical.

values.name: eventTypeFromString
values.comment:
Parse a stored `event_type` string back into an [`AuthEventType`](#AuthEventType),
returning `Nothing` for an unrecognized value. Inverse of
[`eventTypeToString`](#eventTypeToString).

values.name: eventTypeToString
values.comment:
The stable string stored in the `event_type` column for an
[`AuthEventType`](#AuthEventType).

values.name: get
values.comment: Read a single auth event by `id`, returning `Nothing` when no such row exists.

values.name: insert
values.comment:
Insert an auth-event row into the `auth_events` table using caller-supplied
values.
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> { id : String.String, userId : Maybe.Maybe String.String, eventType : String.String, occurredAt : Basics.Int, metadata : Maybe.Maybe String.String } -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error Sqlite.ExecutionSummary

values.name: update
values.comment:
Update an auth event's `event_type` and `metadata` by `id`.

Provided for completeness; mutating an audit record is atypical.
values.type: { id : String.String, eventType : String.String, metadata : Maybe.Maybe String.String } -> Sqlite.Database -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error Sqlite.ExecutionSummary

Auth.Simple.Session.name: Auth.Simple.Session

aliases.name: Session
aliases.comment:
A row from the `sessions` table. `revokedAt` is `Nothing` for a live session
and `Just` the revocation time once it has been explicitly revoked.
aliases.type: { id : String.String, userId : String.String, createdAt : Basics.Int, expiresAt : Basics.Int, lastUsedAt : Basics.Int, revokedAt : Maybe.Maybe Basics.Int }

values.name: create
values.comment:
Open a new session for `userId`, expiring at `expiresAt`, and save it.

Generates a random token, stores only its SHA-256 hash as the row `id`, and
returns `{ session, token }`: the stored [`Session`](#Session) plus the raw
`token` for the client's cookie. The raw token is never persisted. To insert
inside an existing transaction with caller-supplied values, use
[`insert`](#insert) (passing an already-hashed `id`).
values.type: { userId : String.String, expiresAt : Basics.Int } -> Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error { session : Auth.Simple.Session.Session, token : String.String }

values.name: delete
values.comment:
Hard-delete a session by its raw token. To keep the row for auditing, set 
`revoked_at` via [`update`](#update) instead. The `token` is mapped to the 
stored id via [`hashTokenString`](#hashTokenString) before matching.
values.type: String.String -> Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error Sqlite.ExecutionSummary

values.name: encodeToken
values.comment:
Encode raw token bytes into the cookie string handed to the client. Inverse
of [`decodeToken`](#decodeToken).

values.name: generateTokenBytes
values.comment:
Generate a fresh session token: 32 cryptographically-random bytes. These are
the canonical token — [`encodeToken`](#encodeToken) turns them into a string,
[`hashToken`](#hashToken) into the stored id.

values.name: getByToken
values.comment:
Read a single session by its raw token, returning `Nothing` when no row
matches. The token is mapped to the stored id via
[`hashTokenString`](#hashTokenString) before matching.
values.type: String.String -> Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error (Maybe.Maybe Auth.Simple.Session.Session)

values.name: hashToken
values.comment:
Hash raw token bytes into the value stored in `sessions.id`.

Tokens are full-entropy random bytes, so a single SHA-256 (no salt, no stretching)
makes the stored value useless as a cookie while staying reproducible for lookups.

values.name: insert
values.comment: Insert a session row into the `sessions` table using caller-supplied values.
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> { id : String.String, userId : String.String, createdAt : Basics.Int, expiresAt : Basics.Int, lastUsedAt : Basics.Int, revokedAt : Maybe.Maybe Basics.Int } -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error Sqlite.ExecutionSummary

values.name: update
values.comment:
Update a session's mutable fields, identified by its raw token.

Covers both "touch on use" (bump `lastUsedAt`) and revocation (set `revokedAt`).
Pass `Nothing` for `revokedAt` to keep the session live. `expiresAt` extends or
shortens the lifetime. The `token` is mapped to the stored id via
[`hashTokenString`](#hashTokenString) before matching.
values.type: { token : String.String, expiresAt : Basics.Int, lastUsedAt : Basics.Int, revokedAt : Maybe.Maybe Basics.Int } -> Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error Sqlite.ExecutionSummary

Auth.Simple.User.name: Auth.Simple.User

aliases.name: User
aliases.type: { id : String.String, createdAt : Basics.Int, updatedAt : Basics.Int }

values.name: create
values.comment:
Create a new user and save it to the database.

Generates a fresh `id` and timestamp, inserts the row (with `created_at` and
`updated_at` both set to now), and returns the created [`User`](#User). To insert
inside an existing transaction with a caller-supplied `id` and timestamp, use
[`insert`](#insert) directly.

values.name: delete
values.comment:
Delete a user by `id`.

Foreign keys reference `users(id)`, so deleting a user cascades to its sessions,
usernames, and password rows (and sets `auth_events.user_id` to null) per the
schema in [`Auth.Simple`](Auth.Simple).

values.name: get
values.comment: Read a single user by `id`, returning `Nothing` when no such row exists.

values.name: insert
values.comment:
Insert a user row into the `users` table, using the given `id` and
`createdAt` timestamp. Both `created_at` and `updated_at` are set to `createdAt`.
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> { id : String.String, createdAt : Basics.Int } -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error Sqlite.ExecutionSummary

values.name: update
values.comment:
Touch a user, bumping its `updated_at` to the current time.

The minimal `users` schema has no other mutable column, so updating a user means
refreshing its `updated_at` timestamp. Consumers that have extended the table
with their own columns should write their own update queries for those.

Auth.Simple.UsernamePassword.name: Auth.Simple.UsernamePassword

unions.name: CreateError
unions.comment:
Errors that can happen when creating a user with [`create`](#create).

`UsernameBlank` and `PasswordTooShort` are input-validation failures, caught
before anything is hashed or written. `UsernameTaken` comes from an explicit
existence check (a username lookup) before the write, so a sign-up form can tell
the user the name is in use.

unions.name: HashPasswordError
unions.comment: Errors that can happen when creating a hashed password `String`.

unions.name: LoginError
unions.comment:
The single failure a username login surfaces to a caller, plus genuine
database faults.

`InvalidCredentials` deliberately collapses every credential-level failure —
unknown username, no password on file, and wrong password — into one
indistinguishable result. Telling them apart would let an attacker enumerate
which usernames exist. `LoginDatabaseError` is reserved for real infrastructure
failures, which are not a statement about the credentials.

unions.name: VerifyError
unions.comment: Errors that can happen when verifying a user's password with [`verify`](#verify).

unions.name: VerifyPasswordError
unions.comment:
Errors that can happen when verifying a password against a stored PHC
`String`.

values.name: create
values.comment:
Create a user with a username and password and save it to the database,
returning the new user's `userId`.

`password` is a plain-text password. This function handles properly hashing
it before saving to the database, and rejects passwords shorter than
[`minimumPasswordLength`](#minimumPasswordLength).

Input is validated first (see [`validateRegistration`](#validateRegistration)): a
blank username or too-short password fails fast as a [`CreateError`](#CreateError),
before any hashing or database work. The username is stored normalized (see
[`normalizeUsername`](#normalizeUsername)).

Next it checks whether the (normalized) username is already taken with a lookup
via [`Auth.Simple.Identifier.Username.getByUsername`](Auth.Simple.Identifier.Username),
failing with `UsernameTaken` if so. This is a separate round trip ahead of the
write; the `usernames.username` UNIQUE constraint remains the backstop that keeps
a duplicate from ever being created under a concurrent race.

On valid, available input, a single transaction inserts the new user (`users`),
their username (`usernames`), and their hashed password (`passwords`), and records
a `user_registered` event (`auth_events`). It does **not** open a session:
registration and login are separate steps, so the user must log in via
[`verify`](#verify) to obtain a session token.
values.type: { username : String.String, password : String.String } -> Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> Task.Task Auth.Simple.UsernamePassword.CreateError { userId : String.String }

values.name: hashPassword
values.comment:
Properly hash a password, returning a PHC-formatted `String` ready to
safely save to a database.

values.name: login
values.comment:
Log in with a `username` and `password`, opening a session on success.

This is the entry point a login form maps onto: it resolves the `username` to its
`userId` via [`Auth.Simple.Identifier.Username.getByUsername`](Auth.Simple.Identifier.Username),
then defers to [`verify`](#verify). Identity lives on `userId`, so `verify` stays
identifier-agnostic and this function is the thin resolution layer on top.

Every credential-level failure returns `InvalidCredentials`. When the username is
unknown we still run a throwaway password hash before failing, so the unknown-user
path costs the same as the wrong-password path and the two can't be told apart by
timing.

The username is run through [`normalizeUsername`](#normalizeUsername) before the
lookup, matching how [`create`](#create) stored it, so case and surrounding
whitespace don't change which account a login resolves to.
values.type: { username : String.String, password : String.String } -> Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> Task.Task Auth.Simple.UsernamePassword.LoginError { session : Auth.Simple.Session.Session, token : String.String }

values.name: minimumPasswordLength
values.comment:
The minimum password length [`create`](#create) enforces: **8 characters**.

This is a baseline floor, not a full password policy. A consumer wanting stricter
or categorical rules — a longer minimum, character classes, breach-list checks, and
so on — should validate them in the application before calling `create`; those
rules are intentionally not modelled here.

values.name: verify
values.comment:
Verify a `password` for `userId` and, on success, open a fresh session.

Looks up the user's stored (PHC-formatted) password and compares it via
[`verifyPassword`](#verifyPassword). On a match, opens a session and records a
`user_logged_in` event. A wrong password records a `login_failed` event and fails
with `VerificationFailed PasswordMismatch`. No stored password fails with
`NoPasswordForUser`.
values.type: { userId : String.String, password : String.String } -> Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> Task.Task Auth.Simple.UsernamePassword.VerifyError { session : Auth.Simple.Session.Session, token : String.String }

values.name: verifyPassword
values.comment:
Check a plain-text `password` against a stored PHC `String`, succeeding with
`{}` when they match and failing with a [`VerifyPasswordError`](#VerifyPasswordError)
otherwise.

The stored string carries everything needed to reproduce its own hash: the salt,
the iteration count, and the digest algorithm. We parse those back out, re-derive
the hash through the same [`hashPasswordHelper`](#hashPasswordHelper) used to
create it, and compare the result to the stored string. A match proves the
password is the one that produced the stored hash.
